name: How AKU Unlocked Lilian's Vision for Teacher Education

content.title: How AKU Unlocked Lilian's Vision for Teacher Education
content.summary: The Ugandan educator returns from Cambridge with a renewed sense of motivation

media.caption: Lilian Kabahweza gains global perspective through Cambridge's International Summer Programme
media.alt: How AKU Unlocked Lilian's Vision for Teacher Education

content.text: In July 2025, Lilian Kabahweza, a teacher educator from Nakaseke Core Teachers College in Central Uganda, walked through the historic gates of the University of Cambridge. It was her first time as an international student, and the feeling was surreal - stepping into a world where centuries of learning meet the future of innovation.

Lilian joined the International Summer Programme (ISP), a globally recognized academic experience supported by the Aga Khan University's Institute for Educational Development, East Africa (IED,EA). Over four enriching weeks, she engaged in rigorous academic study, cultural exploration, and international networking at one of the world's most prestigious universities.

She immediately connected with the experience. "It was truly a home away from home," Lilian said. "The programme reminded me that learning never stops, it grows with every conversation, every idea, and every new perspective."

At Cambridge, Lilian enrolled in a set of interdisciplinary courses reflecting her passion for inquiry, including Philosophy of Mind, Materials and Our Environment, and How to Think Like an Engineer. Each class offered fresh insights, from understanding human thought and learner diversity to exploring sustainability and creative problem-solving.

"Every course connected deeply with my work as a teacher educator," she explained. "I now think more critically about inclusivity, reflective teaching, and how different disciplines shape the way we approach education."

Her learning extended beyond the classroom. She attended 27 evening talks and plenary lectures led by Cambridge professors, where pressing global issues - from climate change and ethics to the shifting world order - were discussed. Each discussion challenged her to apply global knowledge to her local context in Uganda, inspiring her to integrate these broad perspectives into local teacher training and professional development.

Beyond academics, Lilian embraced the rich cultural and social learning, attending formal dinners and visiting sites like Ely Cathedral. It was the connections, however, that truly defined the experience. "These interactions offered a unique way to connect with people from all over the world and learn how culture shapes teaching and learning," she said. "It was a true classroom without walls."

Returning home, Lilian feels renewed, equipped with new ideas and confidence to inspire her peers and future teachers at Nakaseke Core Primary Teachers' College. She is now focused on designing more inclusive and reflective teaching approaches. "The ISP has strengthened my sense of purpose as an educator," she said. "It reminded me that education is not only about content but about curiosity, compassion, and the courage to think differently."
